**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Subject: Religious Studies (code 0785), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Paper 2: The Old Testament/Jewish Bible and World Faiths. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from any ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Sections of the paper: 1.0 The Old Testament/Jewish Bible, Section 1.1 The Patriarchs to David (questions 1 to 6); Section 5.3 Islam (questions 7 to 12); Section 5.5 African Traditional Beliefs and Practices (questions 13 to 18).

À faire relire par un spécialiste des études religieuses avant mise en avant.

questions.enonce_markdown: Analyse the concept of divinity in ATR. (25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** In African Traditional Religion (ATR) "divinity" covers a range of spiritual beings that stand above human beings and are worshipped or respected. They are usually arranged in an order, with the Supreme Being at the top. The details differ among peoples, so the following is general.

**1. The Supreme Being.**
- Many African peoples recognise one high God who is creator, sustainer and ruler of the universe: for example Nyame among the Akan, Olodumare among the Yoruba, Chukwu among the Igbo.
- He is regarded as all-powerful, all-knowing, everywhere present, eternal and good, and the guardian of the moral order.
- He is both transcendent (far above the world) and near (in rain, sky and daily life). In many societies he has few shrines or priests, and people approach him through intermediaries, but he is called upon in times of need, in proverbs, names and spontaneous prayers.

**2. Lesser divinities.**
- These are beings with delegated powers connected with natural forces and human concerns (sky, thunder, earth, rivers, farming, war, health). Among the Yoruba they are called orisha. They have shrines, priests, festivals and sacrifices.
- They are considered servants or messengers of the Supreme Being and not rivals to him, although they receive much of the daily worship.

**3. Spirits.** Spirits of nature, in trees, rivers and mountains, are feared or respected, and some may be helpful or harmful.

**4. Ancestors.** The "living dead" are not gods but occupy a position between humans and divinities. They are honoured and consulted, and act as guardians of the family and as intermediaries.

**5. Mystical power.** Some beliefs also recognise impersonal forces that can be used in medicine, charms and magic.

**6. Interpretation.** European observers once called this polytheism or animism. African scholars, such as Idowu, argue instead for a "diffuse monotheism": one supreme God, with the other beings dependent upon Him. Others stress the real importance of the divinities in daily worship.

**Conclusion.** The concept of divinity in ATR is a layered one: a supreme creator, divinities with delegated authority, spirits and revered ancestors, all within a religious worldview in which the world is under spiritual governance.
